newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Unheeded Holocaust courier back in Germany.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Unheeded Holocaust courier back in Germany.

text.p: For five decades the man who brought the Allies news of the Nazis' plans to exterminate Europe's Jews, but whom, tragically, no one heeded, refused to visit Germany.

As a Polish resistance fighter, Jan Karski provided the World War Two Allies with the first reliable eyewitness report of the Holocaust while the crime was still going on. But his hopes that they might halt the slaughter were in vain.

"I hated Germany. My wife, who is Jewish and lost her whole family in the Holocaust, said she would never set foot in this country again. But now things have changed and Germany has become an important democratic state," he said.

Karski, now 82, returned to Germany this month at the invitation of the Jewish community to give talks and join Germans in commemorating victims of the Holocaust -- marked by a national memorial day on January 27.

"The last time I was in Berlin was 1942. I was on my way to London with false papers. At the time I came here as an enemy of Germany," said Karski, a Catholic who became a courier for the resistance because of his knowledge of languages.
Karski travelled to London and back three times on a dangerous mission to provide information to the Polish government in exile, surviving capture and torture twice at the hands of the Gestapo.
In 1942 he was asked to go again, this time by the Jewish underground resistance in Poland who asked him to carry an urgent message to the Allies, imploring them for help.
"I had my duty. I didn't think any more about emotions. I had to go. The danger and unpleasantness and hunger were already a way of life in Poland throughout the war," he said.
JEWISH RESISTANCE WANTED ALLIES TO PUBLICISE WAR CRIMES

Jewish resistance leaders wanted the Allies to publicise the Nazis' crimes and warn the German people they would be held accountable after the war. They also wanted the Pope to threaten Catholics who took part in them with excommunication.

To make his account authentic, they smuggled Karski into the Warsaw Ghetto, where only about 50,000 of the original population of 450,000 were still alive. The rest had been transported to the death camps.

Posing as a Ukrainian guard he also visited a concentration camp in eastern Poland. The sights were so horrendous he had a momentary breakdown and, weeping hysterically, would have been caught had he not been quickly smuggled out.
He had to choke off his emotions. "I had no feelings, I was an automaton, a tape recorder," he said. "If I had had feelings, I would have gone mad a hundred times."

Karski left Poland with a 40-page microfilmed report welded inside a key and made his way to the south of France. A Basque communist escorted him over the Pyrenees to Spain and eventually to Gibraltar, from where he flew to London.
He urged the Allies to step up efforts to help Jews escape from Nazi-controlled territories and to bomb Germany in reprisal for the mass murder, but to no avail.
REFUSAL TO BELIEVE HIM
The British foreign secretary Sir Anthony Eden met Karski, but would not even let him speak about the plight of the Jews. He said the matter was being taken care of.
In Washington the response was similar:
"When I mentioned the Jews to (U.S. Secretary of War) Henry Stimson he interrupted me very gently...then he asked me questions, none concerning the Jews," Karski said.
The U.S. president Franklin Roosevelt was primarily interested in politics but told Karski: "The guilty ones will be punished for their crimes."
Even Felix Frankfurter, a Jewish judge at the U.S. Supreme Court, told him: "I just can't believe you."

After the war Karski stopped talking. "I kept silent for 30 years," he said. It was only when Claude Lanzmann asked him to relate his experiences in the 1978 documentary film "Shoah" that he finally broke his silence.
After the war, Karski was honoured by Israel as a "righteous gentile" and had a distinguished academic career at Washington's Georgetown University.
During his German visit, Karski went to the Wannsee Villa outside Berlin where, 55 years ago this month, Hitler made plans for the systematic extermination of the Jews, the "Final Solution".
He was also visiting Munich, Bonn and Cologne to give talks and join in discussions with politicians and Jewish leaders.
"The Jews live with an open wound that does not heal. I live with that same wound. I've seen too much," he said.
The leader of Berlin's Jewish community, Jerzy Kanal, who survived the Warsaw Ghetto, told a news conference:
"It is characteristic of the Jews that they don't forget the wrong done to them. But we also don't forget the people who did their best to save the Jews."

Despite having risked his life behind enemy lines many times, Karski is modest when asked what he thinks his greatest achievement was. "My role during the war is very often exaggerated...Thousands of others perished, I survived."
